info.name: TRA — Service-to-service authentication
info.description:
# Service-to-service authentication

Three services: an auth service, a caller (service A) and a protected resource (service B).

A long lived **application secret** is exchanged for a short lived, audience-bound **access token** at `POST /oauth/token`. That is the only request in the system carrying a secret. Everything downstream carries the token, which service B verifies by calling `POST /oauth/introspect`.

## Getting started

1. Select the **TRA — local** environment (top right).
2. Fill in `adminKey` and `clientSecret`, or generate the environment pre-filled with `npm run postman:env`.
3. Run **1. Health** to confirm the services are up.
4. Run **2. OAuth → Get access token**. It saves `accessToken`, which every service-b request then uses.

Folders 1-5 are the runtime flow; 6-8 are the management API. Requests that are meant to fail say so in their name, and their tests assert the failure — so *Run collection* should come out green end to end.

> **Running the whole collection mutates state.** It creates and then deletes a `billing-worker` application, and it issues, rotates and revokes secrets on `{{appId}}`. Safe against a local stack; think before pointing it at anything shared.

## Variables

| Variable | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `authUrl`, `serviceAUrl`, `serviceBUrl` | Where each service listens |
| `adminKey` | `ADMIN_API_KEY` from `packages/auth-service/.env` |
| `clientId`, `clientSecret` | From `packages/service-a/.env` |
| `accessToken`, `introspectToken` | Filled in by the OAuth requests |
| `appId`, `secretId`, `newAppId`, `newSecretId` | Filled in by the admin requests |

item.name: 1. Health
item.description: Unauthenticated liveness probes. Start here to confirm all three services are up.

item.name: 2. OAuth — secret to token
item.description:
The exchange at the heart of the design. `POST /oauth/token` is the only endpoint in the whole system that accepts an application secret; everything downstream carries the short lived token it returns.

Run **Get access token** first — it saves `accessToken` into the environment, which every service-b request below then uses.

request.description:
Credentials go in the Authorization header as HTTP Basic. The token comes back scoped to one audience and expires in minutes.

Saves `accessToken` for the rest of the collection.

exec: pm.test('token is opaque, not a JWT', () => pm.expect(body.access_token).to.match(/^tra_at_[0-9a-f]{16}\./));

request.description:
A token for the auth service itself. This is what a resource server uses to call `/oauth/introspect` — so even verification never sends a secret.

Saves `introspectToken`.
The RFC 6749 alternative to Basic auth. Sending both at once is rejected rather than silently resolved.

RFC 7662. What service B calls on every request (cached for 30s).

The response carries the calling application's registry profile — team, owner, environment, tags, metadata — which the caller cannot forge because it never touches it.

Requires **Get introspection token** to have run.

A throwaway token for the revocation demonstration below, so the `accessToken` the rest of the collection depends on stays alive.

Saves `disposableToken`.
RFC 7009. Always answers 200 whether or not the token existed, so it cannot be used to probe for valid tokens.

Now inactive. Revocation is immediate at the auth service because the token is opaque and has to be checked here — a signed JWT would stay valid until it expired.

`active: false` covers every failure mode (expired, revoked, malformed, unknown), so probing this endpoint reveals nothing.

item.name: 3. Rejections — what failure looks like
item.description: Each request here is expected to fail, and the test asserts the failure. Together they are the authorisation model stated as behaviour.

request.description: A wrong secret, an unknown application and a malformed credential all return this same response. The endpoint also burns one scrypt verification on the failure path so response timing does not leak whether the application exists.
Indistinguishable from a wrong secret, on purpose.

item.name: Audience the app may not call (403)

request.description: An application can only request tokens for audiences on its `allowedAudiences` list.
`allowedScopes` is a ceiling, not a grant: a request may ask for a subset of it, never more. The demo service-a is read only.
Resource endpoints require a bearer token.
Tokens are opaque, so nothing can be forged from the format alone — the auth service is the only thing that can say a token is real.
A token minted for `tra-auth` is refused by service B. This is what stops a service replaying the tokens it receives against a third party.
Authentication succeeded; authorisation did not. `POST /orders` needs `orders:write`, which the token does not carry.

item.name: 4. Service B — the protected resource
item.description:
Called directly with a bearer token. Service B introspects it at the auth service before any controller code runs.

Run **2. OAuth → Get access token** first.

request.description: Everything service B knows about the caller. The most useful endpoint when wiring up a new client: it shows exactly which registry fields and scopes arrived with the token.
Requires `orders:read`. Visibility is scoped by the caller's `metadata.tenantId` from the registry — not by anything in the request — so a service cannot reach another tenant's data by asking.
Order 2001 belongs to `other-tenant`. The caller is registered under `tdra`, so service B refuses.
Filtered to the caller's tenant.

Returns 403 with the seeded service-a credentials. To see it succeed, add `orders:write` to the application's `allowedScopes` (see **5. Applications → Update application**), then request a new token with `scope=orders:read orders:write`.

item.name: 5. Service A — the caller
item.description: Service A holds its own secret and turns it into tokens on demand, so none of these requests take a credential. Each one triggers the full chain: secret → token → call to service B → introspection → response.

item.name: Fetch an order through service A

request.description: The end-to-end path, in one request.

item.name: What service B sees about service A

request.description: The registry profile that travels with the token, as service B receives it.
Service A passes service B's status code through rather than flattening it into a 500, so you see the real 403.
Forces the next call to mint a fresh token. Use after rotating service A's secret.

item.name: 6. Admin — Applications
item.description:
The registry. Everything written here reaches resource servers with the token, so this is where you describe a caller well enough for service B to make decisions about it — and for an on-call engineer to know who to contact.

Authenticated with `x-admin-key`. This is a different trust domain from service traffic: it creates the credentials everything else depends on.

request.description:
`metadata` is free-form: put whatever a resource server needs to route, meter or restrict this caller.

`allowedAudiences` is which services it may request tokens for. `allowedScopes` is the ceiling on what it can ever be granted.

With `?issueSecret=true` the response includes the plaintext secret — once. It is stored only as a scrypt hash and cannot be recovered.

Saves `newAppId` and `newSecretId`.
All filters are optional; enable the ones you need.
Returns the registry entry, a summary of its secrets (metadata only, never hashes) and how many live tokens it currently holds.

Changes reach resource servers as soon as their introspection cache turns over — 30 seconds by default. Widening `allowedScopes` does not change tokens already issued; those carry the scopes they were minted with.
Reversible kill switch: no new tokens, and every outstanding token is revoked. The audit history survives.
Prefer suspend. Deletion removes secrets and tokens but keeps the audit trail.

item.name: 7. Admin — Secrets
item.description:
An application may hold up to five secrets at once. That is what makes rotation possible without a moment where nothing works.

These requests act on `{{appId}}` (default `service-a`). Run **Issue secret** first to populate `{{secretId}}`.

> **These change real credentials.** Issue, rotate and revoke take effect immediately on whichever application `{{appId}}` names. Harmless against a local stack; point `authUrl` at a shared environment and you are rotating that environment's credentials for real.

request.description:
Send `ttlDays`, or `expiresAt` for an exact instant (it wins if both are present). `ttlDays: 0` means no expiry and is discouraged.

The plaintext is in the response once and never again.

Saves `secretId`.
Metadata only — status, expiry, `lastUsedAt`, `useCount`. Use it to find stale credentials before revoking them, and to confirm a rotation has taken effect.

Issues the replacement immediately and puts the old secret on a countdown, so a running fleet can pick up the new value without a gap. `graceMinutes: 0` revokes the old one at once.

Rotation never extends a secret's life: an earlier expiry stands.

Saves the new id as `secretId`.

exec: console.log('old secret stops working at: ' + body.previous.stopsWorkingAt);

request.description:
Shorten the life of a suspect credential, or extend one about to lapse before a rotation can be scheduled. Send `ttlDays`, or `expiresAt` for an exact instant, or `"expiresAt": null` to clear the expiry entirely (discouraged).

A revoked secret cannot be revived this way.

Break-glass path. The secret stops working at once and every access token it minted is revoked with it — `revokedTokens` in the response tells you how many. Resource servers stop honouring those tokens once their introspection cache turns over.

item.name: 8. Admin — Audit
item.description: Append-only record of everything that touches credentials. Without it, "which service used the leaked secret, and when" has no answer.

request.description:
Newest first. Event types: `token.issued`, `token.denied`, `token.throttled`, `token.revoked`, `secret.issued`, `secret.rotated`, `secret.revoked`, `secret.expired`, `secret.expiry_changed`, `app.created`, `app.updated`, `app.suspended`, `app.activated`, `app.deleted`.

Admin actions are recorded under an `admin:<fingerprint>` actor — the key itself never appears.
After a leak, this is the input to deciding what was actually done with the credential: every token issued from it, with source IP and timestamp. Filter the response by `secretId`.
